claim: In Llama-2-7B-Chat and Llama-3-8B-Instruct, the safety signal that remains after successful jailbreaks is sustained in part by a distinct population of mid-layer attention heads, while attack-sensitive refusal heads are suppressed by jailbreak-template tokens rather than by the harmful request itself. The proposition is supported only if suppressing the persistent heads during successful jailbreaks reduces mean absolute mid-layer safety activation by at least 10% relative to leaving them intact, and if, when each head’s activation is attributed to input tokens, harmful-request tokens drive the two populations in the same direction while template tokens drive them in opposite directions.

experiments: Build the paired evaluation sets used to compare refused harmful requests with successful jailbreaks. Sample benign instructions from Alpaca, collect harmful instructions from multiple published harmful-behavior datasets, and generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking, and PAIR for Llama-2-7B-Chat and Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Retain only one-to-one pairs for which the original harmful request is refused and the attacked variant succeeds. From approximately 10,000 attack samples, 378 pairs for Llama-2-7B-Chat and 176 pairs for Llama-3-8B-Instruct pass this filter, a reported yield of approximately 2–3%.

Extract the refusal feature and fix the head-classification rule. Compute a difference-in-means refusal direction from simple harmful and benign instruction sets, select the best layer on a validation set, and normalize the resulting direction. The selected layer is 12 for Llama-3-8B-Instruct and 14 for Llama-2-7B-Chat. Back-project that direction through attention-head OV circuits, collect each head's end-of-instruction activation score on benign, refused harmful, and successful-attack inputs, estimate activation distributions with KDE using Scott's rule, and set both the harmful-versus-benign and harmful-versus-attack overlap thresholds to 0.5. Standardize each head's activation against its benign mean and standard deviation; among harmful-versus-benign discriminative heads, classify a low-overlap harmful-versus-attack head as an ACH when its standardized activation decreases under attack and as an SAH when it increases.

Identify the attention-head populations whose behavior differs under attack. Apply the two-stage overlap rule with τ_harmful=0.5 and τ_attack=0.5 to 416 heads in layers 0–12 of Llama-3-8B-Instruct and 480 heads in layers 0–14 of Llama-2-7B-Chat. Llama-3 yields 80 harmful-salient heads, 21 ACHs, and 17 SAHs; Llama-2 yields 43 harmful-salient heads, 20 ACHs, and 19 SAHs. More than 60% of ACHs occur in layers 0–3, while SAHs are distributed mainly through layers 5–12. Attack inputs produce both strongly decreased early-layer activations and strongly increased middle-layer activations rather than a uniform reduction.

Test whether SAHs supply part of the refusal activation that remains after a successful attack. Apply the same suppression intervention to SAHs on successful attack inputs and measure mean absolute activation across middle-layer heads, using layers 12–25 for Llama-3-8B-Instruct and layers 14–25 for Llama-2-7B-Chat. For Llama-3, mean absolute activation decreases from 0.0062 without SAH ablation to 0.0053 with ablation, a 14% drop; the corresponding value on original harmful inputs is 0.0086. For Llama-2, it decreases from 0.222 to 0.181, an 18% drop; the original-harmful value is 0.397.

Determine which tokens produce the different ACH and SAH responses. Decompose each head's end-of-instruction activation into additive standardized token contributions using its attention weights and value-vector projection, then separately sum contributions from the original harmful-request tokens and from the jailbreak-template tokens. On original harmful tokens, ACH and SAH activation medians are within ±0.15 for both Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Llama-2-7B-Chat. Jailbreak-template tokens instead produce a median contribution of approximately −1.5 for ACHs and approximately +1.5 for SAHs, a separation exceeding three standard deviations.
